title: Capacity Planning for Architecture
overview: Capacity planning answers two questions: how much extra capacity will the system need, and when must it be in place. The deck gives one three-part recipe (predict the workload, relate workload to resource use, derive the resources needed) and applies it to disk, which is cumulative and trend driven, and to servers, which are peak driven and sized with benchmarks. It adds the forecasting formulas (linear regression, moving average, exponential smoothing), the scalability laws (Amdahl, USL), a worked benchmark-to-throughput example, procurement lead time and cloud elasticity. For the exam, expect to compute a forecast or a sizing figure and justify the method.
big_ideas: Capacity planning combines a **workload forecast** with a measured **workload-to-resource relationship** to predict how much capacity is needed and when.
**Disk is cumulative-driven; servers are peak-driven.** Disk is forecast with trend analysis; servers are sized from benchmarks, load tests and monitoring.
Linear regression: **Y = a + bX**. Moving average: **M_t = (X_t + X_t-1 + ... + X_t-N+1) / N**. Exponential smoothing: **s_t = alpha x_(t-1) + (1 - alpha) s_(t-1)**, s_0 = x_0.
Scaling is **non-linear**: doubling machines does not double throughput. Amdahl's law: **S(N) = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/N)**; USL adds a crosstalk term so throughput can fall as N grows.

The lecture’s simplified benchmark estimate divides reference throughput by scenario slowness, then weights those values by the mix to obtain **38.8 tps**. Validate that estimate with representative mixed-load testing.
Real data beats guesses: use vendor benchmarks, self-benchmarking, or historical monitoring, and measure over enough time to catch patterns, seasonality and time zones.
**Procurement lead time** (7 weeks in the deck's template, plus downtime approval) must go in the project plan: too late means no capacity, too early means paying more because prices fall.
Elasticity: scale up **aggressively**, scale down **conservatively**, and avoid the ping-pong effect by keeping the thresholds apart.

sections.title: Why and how to plan capacity
sections.summary: The goal, the three-part prediction model, where the data comes from and what to measure.

items: Make sure **enough computing resources** exist for the **expected workload**

items.t: Needed for a **new system** and for an **existing one** facing:

items: **Predict the required resources** from the expected workload
**Decide how much extra capacity to buy and when** it is needed (**servers**, **storage**)
**Let the system scale automatically** with workload (**elasticity**)

notes.foot: For **storage** this may be **record count x bytes/record**; for **servers** use **measured workload** and **resource demand**. The relationship is **not literally addition of unlike units**.
**Monitoring is the best source** when a system is already running.

sub: photos uploaded per day (daily and cumulative)

terms.def: Ensuring enough resources for the expected workload at an acceptable service level.
Business-level measure (e.g. photos uploaded per hour) that drives resource demand.

check.q: A photo app expects 50,000 uploads a day at an average of 3 MB, and keeps 3 copies of each photo. Apply the capacity-planning model to estimate storage growth.

items: **Workload-to-resource relationship**: 3 MB x 3 copies = **9 MB per upload**
**Derived capacity**: about **450 GB a day** (decimal units), or roughly **164 TB a year**
a.foot: Each input is an **assumption to monitor**: if the upload rate or photo size grows, the estimate scales with it.

check.q: CPU graphs have risen steadily for months. The business asks what happens if sign-ups double. Can you answer from the system metrics alone?

items: You need **application-level metrics**: sign-ups, uploads, API calls per key
**How each relates to resource use** → turn a **business forecast** into a **resource forecast**
**Start collecting** them alongside the system metrics, and **fit the relationship from history**

check.q: A new system has no production data yet, and the vendor publishes a benchmark for similar hardware. Which data source would you use, and what is the risk?

a.lead: **Use the vendor benchmark as a starting point.**
items: **Self-benchmark** the significant scenarios if you can
**Risk**: the vendor's **workload and configuration** differ from yours → its numbers may not transfer
Once the system runs → switch to **monitoring data**, which is the **best source**

steps.label: Predict workload
steps.detail: Forecast users, transactions or requests, e.g. transactions growing from 1 million to 20 million.

steps.label: Workload-to-resource relation
steps.detail: How much disk, CPU or servers one unit of workload consumes, obtained from benchmark, load test or monitoring.

steps.label: Expected resources
steps.detail: The disk, servers and lead time to procure, with a buffer for estimation error.

sections.title: Planning disk capacity
sections.summary: Disk grows cumulatively, so work out data feeds and growth over the retention period and add fixed overhead.

items: Then **forecast data volume** over the **retention period**
**Customer**, **transaction** and **other data** each have their own **count** and **average size**
Add a **baseline** for **OS and database software**
Allow separately for **logs**, **indexes** and any **replicated copies** that grow with usage
Transactions grow from **1 million to 20 million** at **1 MB per record**
Month k has **1M x 1.1^(k-1)** transactions (starting with **month 1 at 1M**)
= **88.50 TB** at **1 MB each** using **decimal units**
notes.foot: This is a **first-24-month accumulation**, not a **lifetime limit**; revisit the **rolling retention window** as arrivals grow.

notes.h: Deck example 3: only a history chart
items: You only know the **past monthly transaction counts**
→ **extrapolate** with **trend analysis from historical data** (next section)

terms.def: Baseline storage independent of workload; growing logs, indexes and replicas require separate allowances.
One source of stored data (customers, transactions...) sized separately.

check.q: An application writes 20 GB of logs a day and must keep them for 90 days. The busiest day so far produced 35 GB. How much log storage do you plan for?

a.lead: **Disk is cumulative**: plan for everything retained over 90 days, not the peak day.
items: **Some days reach 35 GB** → add **headroom** or forecast **growth in the daily rate**
**Plus overhead** for indexes and any replicas

check.q: Transactions start at 1M a month and grow 10% a month, with 24-month retention and 1 MB per record. A teammate estimates 24 x 1M x 1 MB = 24 TB. Do you agree?

items: Monthly volume is a **geometric series**: 1M x (1.1^24 - 1) / 0.1
→ the teammate's figure is **less than a third** of the need
a.foot: **Revisit the forecast** as actual growth is observed.

check.q: After two years, does 24-month retention mean a growing system's storage stops growing?
check.a: Not necessarily. Old records expire, but newer months may contain more records than the months removed. Forecast the sum within the moving 24-month window using the expected arrival growth.

check.q: Your 88.5 TB data estimate covers records only. The database adds indexes of about 30% of data size and keeps one full replica. What is the real storage need?

items: **Plus** the fixed OS and database baseline and a buffer
a.foot: **Size data feeds and overheads separately** and state the assumptions, so each can be revised.

sections.title: Trend analysis and forecasting methods
sections.summary: Classify the demand pattern, then forecast with regression, moving average or exponential smoothing, and answer 'when do we run out?'.

items: **a = [(Sum y)(Sum x^2) - (Sum x)(Sum xy)] / [n(Sum x^2) - (Sum x)^2]**
**Moving average** → uses the **latest N periods** to **smooth variation**
**Simple exponential smoothing** → weights the **latest observation** against the **previous forecast**
Neither simple method alone models **recurring seasonality** or an **ongoing trend** → **examine those patterns explicitly**
Lecture data: **20 daily consumption readings**, from **202 to 280.7 GB**, with **500 GB capacity**
**Fit a model** and **solve for when predicted use reaches 500 GB**
**Linear fit** to those readings → roughly **Y = 194.1 + 4.35X**, reaching **500 GB near day 70** (when **day 1** is the **first observation**)
**Allow forecast error** and **revise with new observations**
notes.foot: **Neither extrapolation reveals the actual future date.**

terms.def: Mean of the last N periods.
Forecast weighting recent data by alpha, older data by (1 - alpha).

check.q: Storage use rises steadily month by month. A different metric, order volume, spikes every December. Which forecasting approach suits each?

items: **Storage is trending** → fit a **regression** (linear or exponential) and extrapolate
**Orders are seasonal** → model the **yearly cycle** explicitly, for example by comparing each December with previous ones
a.foot: A simple **moving average** or **exponential smoothing** would smooth out the December spike rather than predict it.

check.q: After a merger, traffic stepped up permanently by 40%. Your exponential-smoothing forecast with alpha = 0.1 still lags far behind. Why, and what would you change?

items: **Why**: a **low alpha** gives little weight to the latest observation → the forecast adjusts slowly to a real **level change**
**Fix**: **raise alpha** so it reacts faster, or **refit** from the post-merger data
a.foot: A **high alpha** also chases noise, so choose it for how quickly real change happens.

check.q: A linear fit says the disk fills on day 70 and an exponential fit says day 55. Today is day 20, and procurement takes 7 weeks. When do you order?

items: **Linear forecast** leaves **50 days** → almost no margin
a.foot: Both are **extrapolations with error**, so plan on the **earlier date plus a buffer**, and keep comparing the fits with new readings.

visuals.title: Forecasting methods
visuals.caption: Simple smoothing does not itself forecast seasonal cycles or continuing growth. Validate the pattern before extrapolating.

sections.title: Server sizing: benchmarks and mapping
sections.summary: Server capacity is peak driven and sized from benchmarks; the key skill is scaling a reference benchmark to your scenarios.

items: ...under a **varying load** of **clients** and **requests per client**
Ideally run it on the **same machine type** for **each significant scenario**
**Much easier on cloud** than buying hardware
If not possible → estimate a **slowness factor**
Scenario **twice as slow** as the reference → roughly **half the reference throughput**
**Five concurrent transaction types** over **nine table types**
A **published result** = evidence for its **tested workload and configuration**
**Not automatically the capacity of your application**
**App server CPU** stays at **95-98%** at max TPS; **DB server** almost **idle** (**under 1% to 2.25% CPU**)
notes.foot: **Never assume capacity scales linearly with servers.**

terms.def: Running standard tests to assess relative performance of a server.
Industry OLTP benchmark, measured in transactions per minute (tpmC).
How many times slower a scenario is than the reference benchmark.

check.q: A service averages 200 requests/s, peaks at 900 requests/s on Monday mornings, and its data grows by 5 GB a day. How do you size the servers and the disk?

items: **Servers are peak-driven**: size for **900 requests/s** at the response target, plus **headroom for a node failure**; average load is irrelevant to that
**Disk is cumulative**: size for **5 GB a day** over the **retention period**, plus overhead
a.foot: Using the average for servers, or the peak for disk, would get both wrong.

check.q: The benchmark shows 17.04 tps on 1 machine, 30.81 on 2 and 55.76 on 4. A teammate plans 8 machines for 136 tps. Do you agree?

items: → 8 machines might give about **101 tps** if the trend holds, and it may get worse
The **application servers' CPU** was already at **95-98%** at maximum load
a.foot: **Benchmark 8 machines**, or fit a **scalability model**, before committing.

check.q: A reporting scenario is 4 times slower than the reference benchmark of 55.76 tps on 4 machines, and the business needs 30 report requests/s. Is 4 machines enough?

items: **Estimated throughput**: 55.76 / 4 → about **13.9 tps**, less than half the need
a.foot: **Reduce the scenario's cost** (precompute, cache, optimise queries) as well as adding capacity, and **benchmark the actual report**.

check.q: At maximum TPS, the application servers' CPU sits at 97% and the database server's at 2%. A teammate proposes a bigger database server. Respond.

items: The **application tier is the bottleneck**; the database is almost idle
A bigger database adds nothing until the application tier is **scaled out** or made **cheaper per request**
a.foot: **Re-measure** afterwards, because the bottleneck may then **move to the database**.

sections.title: Non-linearity: Amdahl's law and USL
sections.summary: Two models explain why adding servers gives diminishing (or negative) returns and let you predict scaling from a few measurements.

items: **Ceiling = 1 / (1 - P)** however many servers you add
**Measure P** by **load testing** with **increasing numbers of servers**, then **predict**
notes.foot: **Load-test results are very sensitive to workload mix**, so the test must **mimic real usage**.

items: **Fit coefficients to measurements**; do **not infer them from the technology name**

notes.h: Lecture case study: Java vs Node.js
items: Fitted **Java** results → **lower serialisation** but **higher crosstalk** than the **Node.js** implementation
notes.foot: These measurements **compare those systems**; they do **not establish a general language ranking**.

terms.def: Speedup limit set by the serial fraction of work: S(N) = 1/((1-P)+P/N).
USL coefficient for contention; sets the throughput ceiling.
USL coefficient for coherency cost; makes throughput decline beyond a peak.

check.q: A workload is 90% parallel. Going from 10 to 20 servers, how much speedup do you gain, and what is the ceiling?

items: → doubling the servers gives only about **31% more speedup**
a.foot: **Reducing the serial part** pays more than adding servers.

check.q: Throughput rises up to 8 nodes, then falls at 12. Which model explains this, and what does it say about the cause?

a.lead: **USL, not Amdahl**: Amdahl's speedup flattens but never falls.
items: **Cause of the decline**: the **crosstalk (coherency) term, kappa** → nodes spend more and more effort **coordinating** with each other
**Fit sigma and kappa** to the measurements → find the **peak**
**Reduce cross-node coordination** if you need to scale further

check.q: The parallel fraction P was measured with a load test that sent only login requests. Should you trust the resulting scaling prediction?

items: **P depends on the workload mix**: logins may parallelise well, while **checkouts update shared data serially**
**Unrepresentative test** → the wrong P → the wrong server count
a.foot: Repeat the test with a **production-like mix**.

check.q: Load tests show that a single shared stock-count row is updated on every order. How does that affect scaling, and what would you change?

items: **Effect**: every order **serialises** on that row → lowers the **parallel fraction P** → caps speedup at **1 / (1 - P)**
**Change**: **reduce the serial part**, for example by **partitioning** the stock count or updating it **asynchronously**
a.foot: Accept the trade-off in **exactness or consistency** of the count.

visuals.title: Amdahl vs USL
rows: X(N) = gamma N / (1 + sigma(N - 1) + kappa N(N - 1))
gamma slope, sigma serialisation, kappa crosstalk

sections.title: Sizing a system from a benchmark
sections.summary: Reproduce the lecture’s simplified weighted benchmark estimate, state its assumptions and validate the production mix with load testing.

notes.lead: Each scenario gets a factor against the **4-machine reference of 55.76 tps**; **estimated throughput = 55.76 / slowness**.

notes.h: Lecture estimate: weight by workload mix
notes.lead: Multiply each scenario’s **estimated throughput** by its **workload share**:
notes.foot: This is the **deck’s simplified sizing procedure**, **not a general law** for combining **mixed-workload capacities**.

items: A **uniform slowness factor** across **application and database tiers**
notes.foot: **Benchmark it directly** before treating **38.8 tps** as **deployable capacity**.

sub: both let you define **scenarios** and **arrival rates** and give **response time** and **throughput**

items: **With a production server** → **analyse your monitoring data**, which is the **best source**

terms.def: Percentage of traffic made up of each scenario.
Simulating client traffic to measure response time and throughput.

check.q: With the lecture's mix, 4 machines give an estimated 38.8 tps. The forecast peak is 50 tps. How many machines would you plan for?

items: **Linear estimate**: 50 / 38.8 → about **1.29 times** the capacity → about **5.2 machines**
**Scaling has been sub-linear** (about 1.8x per doubling) → plan to **benchmark 6 or more** with the production mix
Then add **headroom for a node failure**
a.foot: The **weighted estimate** is a simplified starting point, not deployable capacity.

check.q: If Payment's share rose from 5% to 10% (taking 5% from Login), what happens to overall throughput?

items: Within the lecture's **weighted estimate**, replacing 5% Login with Payment changes the total by 0.05 x (13.94 - 55.76) = **-2.091 tps**
a.foot: The actual production effect requires **mixed-load measurement**.

check.q: You have neither a reference benchmark nor a production system. How do you get sizing data?

a.lead: **Run simulated load tests** (for example with **JMeter** or **Artillery**).
items: **Define** the scenarios, the mix and the arrival rates
**Measure** response time and throughput as load increases
a.foot: Once a production system exists, switch to its **monitoring data**, which is the best source.

visuals.title: Lecture’s simplified mixed-workload estimate
visuals.caption: Reproduce this method for the lecture exercise; measure representative mixed traffic before relying on the result for deployment.

sections.title: Using existing data and measurement time
sections.summary: Existing monitoring gives the best data, but only if you measure across long enough windows to see patterns.

notes.foot: **Looking at the wrong window gives the wrong peak.**

items: e.g. **US West** and **East** usage curves are **offset**
**Peak usage** (**busy Apache processes**) falls on **Monday every week**
The peak **slowly trends upward**: weekly trendline **y = 42.75x + 726**
**Take the weekly peaks** and apply the **same trend analysis as for storage**

terms.def: Repeating demand pattern tied to time (week, month, year).

check.q: A team sized its servers from a one-hour sample taken on a Tuesday afternoon. What is the risk?

items: **Risk**: the sample hides **daily and weekly cycles**
If the real peak is **Monday morning**, as in the **Flickr** example → servers **undersized** exactly when demand is highest
a.foot: **Measure over weeks**, identify the **recurring peak**, and size for it.

check.q: A service used only in Asia expands to Europe. How might the load pattern change?

items: **Time zones shift and blend the peaks**: the European peak arrives hours after the Asian one
→ the service is busy for **more hours each day**, and the peaks **may overlap**
a.foot: **Re-measure** after the launch, and size for the **combined peak**, not either region alone.

check.q: Monday peak busy processes follow the trend y = 42.75x + 726, where x is weeks. Your servers handle 1,600 busy processes in total, and procurement takes 7 weeks. When do you run out, and when must you order?

items: With a **7-week lead time plus a buffer** → **order by about week 12 or 13**
a.foot: Check the trend against **new weekly peaks**, since a **steeper trend** moves the date earlier.

sections.title: Procurement lead time and elasticity
sections.summary: Buying capacity takes time that must be planned; the cloud shortens it with auto-scaling governed by sensible policies.

items: **Downtime needed** and **lead time to get downtime approved**
notes.foot: All of this goes into the **project plan**; **cloud and automation** can cut much of it.
**Estimated downtime or reduced SLA: 4 hours**, with **1 week lead time** for **downtime approval**.

items: **Early procurement** → **ties up money** and may **miss later price reductions**
Use the **forecast**, **uncertainty**, **actual lead times** and **failure headroom** to plan a **safe date**

items.t: **Cloud providers auto-scale instances** using a policy of:
**Avoid ping-pong**: requests per second per node
sub: after **scaling up** must stay **above the scale-down threshold**
after **scaling down** must stay **below the scale-up threshold**

items: → **be systematic**, so it is **easy to communicate** and **to revise**

terms.def: Time after a scaling action before another is allowed.
Repeated scale up then scale down caused by thresholds set too close.
Scaling at planned times based on historical patterns.

check.q: New instances take 5 minutes to start, and traffic doubles within 3 minutes at 9 am every weekday. How should the scaling work?

a.lead: Use **scheduled scaling** from the historical pattern.
items: **Reactive scaling will always be late** → demand doubles before new instances are ready
**Scale down conservatively** afterwards → briefly holding spare capacity costs little compared with failing users

check.q: Two nodes handle 120 requests/s. Scale-out triggers above 55/node and scale-in below 45/node. Why might adding one node cause ping-pong?

items: **After adding a third**: each handles 40/s → below the 45/s **scale-in threshold**
a.foot: Set **thresholds and adjustments** so the new state does not immediately trigger the opposite action; use **cooldown** as well.

check.q: The forecast says capacity runs out in 6 weeks. The procurement template totals about 7 weeks, plus 1 week to get downtime approved. What do you do now, and what do you change for next time?

a.lead: **You are already late** for the normal process.

sub: Look for **interim capacity**: temporary cloud capacity, expedited delivery, or reducing or throttling demand
**Start procurement immediately**, running the **downtime approval in parallel**

items: **Next time**: trigger procurement from the **forecast** with the **full lead time plus a buffer**
a.foot: Buying very early has its own cost, **tying up money** and **missing price drops**, so plan the date rather than **stockpiling**.

exam_angles.q: A database disk has 280 GB used of 500 GB, and the last 20 days of readings fit a linear trend of about 4.35 GB a day. Procurement takes about 7 weeks, plus 1 week for downtime approval. When does the disk fill, and when must you act? What could make the forecast wrong?

items: **Time to fill**: (500 - 280) / 4.35 → about **51 days**, roughly **7 weeks**
→ the disk fills at about the point a normal **7-week procurement** would deliver
With a **buffer**, and possibly the extra week for **downtime approval** → you must **act now**

sub: Growth may be **exponential rather than linear** → brings the date forward
**Logs and indexes** may grow faster than the data

a.foot: **Compare linear and exponential fits**, keep revising with new readings, and **plan from the earlier date**.

exam_angles.q: Estimate storage for 1 million transactions a month growing 10% a month, retained for 2 years, at 1 MB per record, with indexes adding 30% and one replica. Then explain what happens to storage in year 3.

items: **First 24 months**: 1M x (1.1^24 - 1) / 0.1 → about **88.5M records**, or **88.5 TB**
**Plus** the fixed OS and database baseline and a buffer

sub: But each new month (about **9.8M records** by month 25) is far larger than the month it replaces (**1M**)

a.foot: Forecast the **moving 24-month window**, not a one-off total.

exam_angles.q: The 4-machine reference benchmark gives 55.76 tps. Slowness factors are Login 1.0, Search 2.0, Details 1.5, Cart 1.5, Checkout 2.0 and Payment 4.0, and the mix is 30/20/15/20/10/5%. The forecast peak is 45 tps, and the business wants to survive one machine failure. Estimate the capacity and recommend a machine count.

items: **Weighted estimate**: 16.73 + 5.58 + 5.58 + 7.43 + 2.79 + 0.70 → about **38.8 tps** on 4 machines, short of 45 tps
**Sub-linear scaling** (about 1.8x per doubling) → 45 tps needs more than a proportional **4.6 machines**
**Survive one failure** → the survivors must still deliver 45 tps
If the 1.8x-per-doubling trend holds, **5 machines** give about **47 tps**
→ **plan for 6** (5 survivors after a failure), and confirm it by **benchmarking with the production mix**
a.foot: The estimate assumes **uniform slowness across tiers** and the **benchmark's configuration**, so validate it with a **mixed load test**.

exam_angles.q: Load tests measure 1,000 req/s on 1 node, 1,800 on 2, 3,000 on 4 and 3,200 on 8. Explain the pattern, estimate what 16 nodes would give, and recommend what to do.

items: **Pattern**: returns diminish quickly; 4 to 8 nodes adds only **7%**
**Suggests** a large **serial part** (shared data, quotas) and possibly **crosstalk**

items.t: **16 nodes** may give little or even **less than 3,200 req/s**
sub: **USL** allows throughput to **fall past a peak**
**Fit USL's sigma and kappa** to these points → find the peak
Better value comes from **reducing the serial work**, such as **shared-row updates** or **cross-node coordination**
**Rerun the tests** with a production-like mix

exam_angles.q: Design an auto-scaling policy for a web tier with a Monday 9 am peak of 900 requests/s, nodes that handle 100 requests/s at the response target, and a 3-minute start-up time. Include thresholds that avoid ping-pong.

items: **Scheduled scaling** from the weekly trend → about **10 nodes** before 9 am: 9 for the load, plus 1 for headroom
**React to surprises**: scale up **aggressively**, since start-up takes 3 minutes; scale down **conservatively** with a **cooldown**
**Thresholds**, for example: scale out above **80 requests/s per node**, scale in below **50**

sub: 4 nodes at 80 = 320 requests/s, spread over 5 nodes, gives **64** → above the scale-in threshold
5 nodes at 50 = 250, over 4 nodes, gives **62.5** → below the scale-out threshold
So **neither action immediately triggers the other**

a.foot: **Revisit the thresholds** as the Monday trend grows.
